case_name: Ng v. Manjit International Development Ltd.
text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Ng v. Manjit International Development
Ltd.
,

2010 BCSC 380

Date: 20100324

Docket:
S086327

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Richard Ng

Plaintiff

And

Manjit International Development
Ltd.,

S. Parmar, Frederick W. Chan and Tim
L. Tse

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Willcock

Reasons for Judgment

The Plaintiff, Richard Ng:

Appearing
on his own behalf

The Defendants Manjit International
Development Ltd. and S. Parmar:

S.
Parmar appearing in person

Counsel for Mr. Chan:

D.
Marks

Counsel for Mr. Tse:

D. K.
Plunkett

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

January 28, 2010

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

March 24, 2010

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Tim Song Lee (“Tse”) and Frederick W. Chan
(“Chan”) apply for orders striking out the claims made against them by Richard
Ng (“Ng”) pursuant to Rule 19(24), which provides that at any stage of a
proceeding the court may order to be struck out the whole or part of any
pleading on the grounds that it discloses no reasonable claim, that it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or that it may constitute an
abuse of the process of the court.

BACKGROUND

The Pleadings

[
2
]

Ng’s claim is set out in a statement of claim
most recently amended on September 25, 2008.  Ng is unrepresented and his
pleadings are not clearly drafted. The claim described in the pleadings, in
short, is as follows.

[
3
]

Ng was the owner of property at 3675 and 3677
Wellington Avenue in Vancouver.  In March 2007, Chan, a real estate agent,
introduced Parmar, a contractor and the principal of Manjit International
Development Ltd. (“Manjit”), to Ng.  Ng then retained Manjit to build a duplex
on the property and the building was constructed between May and
November 2007.

[
4
]

Ng alleges that he deposited $20,000 with Chan
to be held in escrow pending completion of the duplex and that on April 2,
2007 Chan “illegally” and without Ng’s consent released those funds to Parmar
and Manjit.  That claim is referred to here as the “escrow claim”.

[
5
]

Ng says that in February 2008, he entered
into a listing agreement with Chan, a real estate agent.  On April 13,
2008, Tse, also a real estate agent, is said to have approached Ng and
represented that he acted for two potential buyers.  Ng says he signed a
contract to sell the property to the potential buyers, subject to their
satisfactory inspection of the property, relying upon the advice and
representations of both Chan and Tse.  That sale did not complete.  Ng claims
to have suffered damages as a result of the falling real estate market.

[
6
]

Ng says the defendants Parmar, Manjit, Chan and
Tse collectively refused to arrange for the inspection of the property by the
buyers.  He further says the defendants were business associates, but “misled
the plaintiff into believing that they had no business dealings among
themselves and therefore deliberately withheld information from the plaintiff”.

[
7
]

The statement of claim, in the following
paragraphs, sets out a very vague description of the cause of action against Tse
and Chan:

[22]      Defendants knew or ought to know
that they have fiduciary obligations towards the plaintiff.

[25]      Defendants Chan and Tse knew or
ought to have known that as realtors, they are statutorily and legally obliged
to deal with the plaintiff with fidelity and fair dealing by disclosing any
conflict of interest and by performing their duties as seller’s and buyer’s
agent in utmost good faith.

[26]        Defendants knew or ought to have
known that their wanton failure or refusal to perform their respective duties
as builders and agents without disclosing to the plaintiff that they are
business associates:

a.         Had
prevented the plaintiff from selling the duplex to prospective buyers;

b.         Had
the effect furthermore of inflicting serious economic harm on the plaintiff.

[27]
Defendants are liable for the consequences of their failure to observe the
statutory and legal standards of care and fair dealing, and the breach of trust
and fiduciary duties towards the plaintiff.

[
8
]

The only specific acts or omissions identified
in the pleadings that might be said to amount to such a breach of duty, aside
from Chan’s payment of the $20,000 deposit to Parmar, are:

The recommendation that he enter into the
April 12, 2008 contract of sale and representations made in relation to
that contract;

The failure to arrange for the inspection of
the property called for under that contract; and

The collective
failure of Tse and Chan to disclose the fact they and Parmar were “business
associates”.

[
9
]

These claims are referred to here as “the
realtor claims”.

Submissions

[
10
]

Tse says in response to allegations against him
that he was not retained by Ng, he owes him no duty of care and no case against
him is disclosed in the pleadings.

[
11
]

Chan says the allegations that are the
foundation of the escrow claim and the realtor claims have been dismissed by a
prior judgment of this Court following a lengthy trial, in an action between
Manjit and Ng (Supreme Court of British Columbia, Vancouver Registry Action
No.  S083456 - the “Manjit Action”) and that an attempt to re-argue these
allegations is an abuse of the process of the Court.

Judgment of March 31, 2009.

[
12
]

In the Manjit Action Wedge J. addressed
three claims:

(a)    a claim brought by Manjit for outstanding amounts owing under
the contract to construct the duplex;

(b)    a claim by Ng that he had mistakenly overpaid Manjit by the
amount of two cheques, one for $100,000 and the other for $20,000; and

(c)     a counterclaim brought by Ng for deficiencies in the
construction and consequential losses said to flow from his inability to sell
the duplex on the anticipated construction completion date in March 2008.

[
13
]

Judgment in that action was pronounced on
March 31, 2009.  The Court allowed Manjit’s claim, after making allowances
for minor deficiencies in the construction, rejected most of Ng’s defence and
dismissed the counterclaim.  In support of his claim that there were
significant deficiencies that had to be rectified before the property could be
listed or sold, Ng produced an invoice for the cost of rectifying deficiencies
from a company called GRI Construction.  After having failed to provide
particulars of the work and denying that he had any connection to that company,
he acknowledged at trial that GRI was a company of which he was the sole
shareholder and a director.  The trial judge held:

[42] It can
fairly be said that Mr. Ng’s credibility concerning the deficiencies was,
by the end of the trial, severely compromised.  I am satisfied beyond any doubt
that he created his own deficiency list and created a fictional quote by a
fictional construction company.  He swore several affidavits in which he
deposed that he had paid $55,000 to this construction company for the rectification
of deficiencies and represented the same to Master Scarth at several case
management conferences.

[
14
]

The claim for overpayment was set out in
paragraph 5 of Ng’s July 14, 2008 amended counterclaim as follows:

On April 1,
2007 the Plaintiff [Manjit] requested the Defendant [Ng] to pay $20,000 deposit
to his agent, Fred Chan, to hold in trust until completion; but the Plaintiff
unilaterally took the $20,000 deposit from Fred Chan on April 2, 2007, the
next day; the Defendant believes that the action of the Plaintiff is fraudulent
and is a conduct of breach of the Contract;

[
15
]

The amended counterclaim of August 9, 2008
advances a slightly different claim in paragraph 11:

The Plaintiff
[Manjit] has wilfully breached the Contract by first having induced a $20,000
deposit to be placed in Fred Chan’s control and then having processed the
deposit without the Defendant’s knowledge and consent at the very instant;
these actions have contravened the terms of the Contract.

[
16
]

The Court rejected Ng’s evidence that he had paid
and Manjit had received the $20,000 cheque.  Prior to trial, upon being unable
to produce documentation in support of alleged overpayments, including the
$20,000 deposit, Ng had suggested he might abandon that claim and pursue it
later.  Wedge J. would not permit Ng to proceed in that fashion, given an
outstanding order to produce the evidence, if any, of the alleged payments.
She advised Ng that he should produce all of his evidence in support of the
alleged payments to Parmar and Manjit and that she would rule on the matter.
Manjit’s banking records and Ng’s banking records were produced and reviewed.
Ng’s account of payments to Manjit was dismissed.  The Court expressly rejected
as untruthful Ng’s evidence that he had overpaid Manjit, taking into account
the disputed cheques:

I am satisfied
that no such overpayment occurred.  I am also satisfied that Mr. Ng
advanced the allegation knowing it to be false in order to prolong the
litigation and discourage Mr. Parmar from pursuing his claim.  Further, Mr. Ng
vigorously advanced the overpayment claim in his application under the Rule 18A
summary trial application.  He appended to the affidavit in support of the 18A
application a letter he had sent to Mr. Parmar in the early days of the
dispute which contradicted his claim for overpayment.  Mr. Ng did a “cut
and paste” of this letter, deleting those portions that were harmful to his
claim, re-photocopied it and appended it to his affidavit, which I have
concluded he swore knowing that what he attested to was false and that he had
altered the document.

[
17
]

The Court then turned to Ng’s counterclaim
founded upon the allegation that a potential sale had been lost due to
deficiencies.  That claim was set out in paragraph 16 of Ng’s July 14,
2008 amended counterclaim (substantially repeated as paragraphs 34-36 of the
amended counterclaim of August 9, 2008) as follows:

On April 13,
2008, two offers were made through Tim Tse, a realtor from Royal Pacific
Realty, to purchase the two half duplexes, and were accepted at the price of
$679,000 each.  There was a subject on each offer which stated that all the
deficiencies must be repaired prior to an inspection on May 1, 2008.  The
deals were collapsed on May 1, 2008 because the Plaintiff had deliberately
refused to do any repair within the time limit and had refused to provide the
keys for inspection.  The Plaintiff has therefore succeeded in stopping the
Defendant from selling the properties and has succeeded in making the said
properties lose their market value in the present recessive market.

[
18
]

That claim was dealt with in the following
terms:

[48]      Mr. Ng alleges that because
of the deficiencies and certain other alleged conduct on the part of
Mr. Parmar, he was unable to sell the duplex in March 2008 once the
occupancy permit was issued.  He alleged that he had buyers for the property in
April 2008 who put an almost full-priced offer on both units, but did not
complete the transaction because of the deficiencies.  Mr. Parmar called
as part of his case the realtor who was retained by these “potential buyers”.
The realtor, Mr. Tse, gave detailed evidence about his dealings with the
buyer, who only ever gave his name as “John”.  I will not recite the evidence
of Mr. Tse in any detail, but suffice to say that Mr. Tse could never
obtain a phone number, a street address, or e-mail address from John.  He could
not even obtain his last name.  John purported to be travelling primarily in
China while he was dealing with Mr. Tse; however, Mr. Tse discovered
John was actually e-mailing him from the Lower Mainland of British Columbia
when he represented to Mr. Tse that he was in China.  John purported to
know about numerous deficiencies in the duplex, yet had never been inside
either units.  He e-mailed a list of deficiencies he wanted addressed before he
would make an unconditional offer on the property.  They were deficiencies
strikingly similar to some of those identifies by Mr. Ng.  The supposed
buyer became increasingly abusive with Mr. Tse when he seemed unable to
assist with the rectification of the deficiencies.  Mr. Tse explained time
and again that that was not his role.  Eventually Mr. Tse terminated the
relationship because he strongly suspected John was not a legitimate purchaser,
and that someone may have been perpetrating a fraud.

[49]      I am
satisfied that John is not a legitimate purchaser.  I am satisfied the person
operating as John was likely Mr. Ng, who was attempting to pressure
Mr. Parmar to rectify any deficiencies he had identified without having to
first pay the final instalment on the contract.  Mr. Ng continued to press
his counterclaim at trial, alleging a
bone fide
purchaser had walked
away from his offer due to the deficiencies.  I have concluded there was no
bona
fide
purchaser.  Nor was there any evidence to suggest the deficiencies in
any way compromised Mr. Ng’s ability to sell the property.

Appeal

[
19
]

That judgment was appealed by Mr. Ng.  The
appeal was dismissed (
2009 BCCA 429
).  The Court of Appeal held as follows:

[7]        The
trial judge dismissed Mr. Ng’s counterclaim because she concluded that
there had not been a bona fide purchaser of the house and the deficiencies did
not compromise Mr. Ng’s ability to sell the property, that the delay of
Manjit Development in completing the construction was outside of its control
and that the alleged $120,000 overpayment had not been made.

[
20
]

After considering Ng’s allegation that the trial
judge had erred in making a finding of fact upon which her credibility findings
rested, the Court of Appeal concluded:

[12]   ...There
was evidence to support her finding of fact in that regard, and there were
several other examples of evidence which supported her conclusion about Mr. Ng’s
credibility generally.  After hearing the testimony of both Mr. Ng and Mr. Parmar
and receiving all of the documentary evidence, the trial judge was entitled to
prefer the evidence of Mr. Parmar over that of Mr. Ng.  The appellant
has failed to demonstrate any palpable and overriding error in the findings
made by the trial judge, and there is no basis for this Court to interfere with
her findings.

[
21
]

The appeal was only allowed to the extent that
the Court reduced the award to the plaintiff Manjit by setting aside an award
made for the cost of building a garage on a quantum merit basis when there was
no pleading upon which such an award could be based.  The Court of Appeal did
not disturb the substantive findings as against Mr. Ng, with respect to
his allegations involving the potential sale of the property and the effect of the
alleged deficiencies upon the marketing of the home.

The Current Status

[
22
]

Thus, there is a finding following a trial, undisturbed
on appeal, that Ng did not pay Manjit any amount in excess of the construction
costs and a finding that he had not lost an opportunity to sell the duplex to
Tse’s clients.  His evidence in relation to these allegations was a concoction unworthy
of credit.  The trial judge concluded that the person posing as a buyer to Tse
was “likely Mr. Ng”.

[
23
]

Ng now, again alleges that he made payments of
$100,000 and $20,000 to Manjit and Parmar, on April 2, 2007.  He says the
former payment was a mistake and the latter a deposit paid out by Chan contrary
to his instructions.  He seeks to recover the latter sum from Chan and seeks
damages for economic loss he says was intentionally or negligently inflicted
upon him by both realtors in relation to April 2008 attempt to sell the
duplex.

[
24
]

His claim against Tse and Chan is said to be for
“breach of contract, fiduciary duty and trust and intentional infliction of
economic harm to the plaintiff”.  The complaint is that the agents concealed
that they were business associates but the only specific act he complains of is
that they made representations and gave advice that led him to enter into the
contract and then failed to arrange for the inspection of the property called
for by the contract.

ISSUE

[
25
]

Should the claims against Tse and Chan be
dismissed on the ground the pleadings disclose no reasonable claim, or, in the
alternative, as vexatious claims or as an abuse of process?

Applicable Law

[
26
]

Rule 19(24) provides:

At any stage of a proceeding the Court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that:

(a)     it discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may
be,

(b)     it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)     it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or
hearing or the proceeding, or

(d)     it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the Court,

and the Court may grant judgment or order
the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

[
27
]

The Rule was cogently summarized by Garson J. in
Dempsey et al.  v. Envision Credit Union et al
.,
2006 BCSC 750
as follows:

[17]      In summary, a pleading will be
struck out if:

(a)     the pleadings are unintelligible, confusing and difficult to
understand (
Citizens for Foreign aid Reform
, (1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266
(B.C.S.C.) at p. 276);

(b)     the pleadings do not establish a cause of action and do not
advance a claim known in law (
Citizens for Foreign aid Reform
, supra);

(c)     the pleadings are without substance in that they are
groundless, fanciful and trifle with the Court’s time (
Borsato v. Basra

2000 BCSC 28 (CanLII)
, [2000]
BCJ No. 84 (S.C.), reversed on other grounds,
2000 BCSC 1898 (CanLII)
, [2000] B.C.J. No. 2855)

(d)     the pleadings are not bona fides, are oppressive and are
designed to cause the Defendants anxiety, trouble and expense (
Borsato v. Basra
,

supra
);

(e)     the action is
brought for an improper purpose, particularly the harassment and oppression of
the Defendants (
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
,
2002 BCSC 466
.

[
28
]

On an application to dismiss a claim pursuant to Rule 19(24)(a)
on the ground that the pleadings do not disclose a reasonable claim the
applicant has the burden of meeting the test set out in
Hunt
v. Carey Canada Inc
.,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at p. 980:

Thus, the test
in Canada governing the application of provisions like Rule 19(24)(a) of the
British Columbia
Rules of Court
is the same as the one that governs an
application under R.S.C.O. 18, r. 19: assuming that the facts as stated in
the statement of claim can be proved, is it “plain and obvious” that the
plaintiff’s statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action?  As in
England, if there is a chance that the plaintiff might succeed, then the
plaintiff should not be “driven from the judgment seat”.  Neither the length
and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of action, nor the
potential for the defendant to present a strong defence should prevent the
plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case.  Only if the action is certain
to fail because it contains a radical defect ranking with the others listed in
Rule 19(24) of the British Columbia
Rules of Court
should the relevant
portions of a plaintiff’s statement of claim be struck out under Rule
19(24)(a).

[
29
]

This test was found to be met in
Budgell v. British
Columbia
,
2007 BCSC 991
(approved at
2008
BCCA 349
) on the basis that a material fact had not been plead.  The
Court held:

[9]  The issue
is not whether the plaintiff has failed to identify the specific causes of
action or tort claims advanced.  Rather, the Court is to examine the statement
of claim to see whether the material facts set out would, if proved, complete
all the constituent elements of causes of action known in law: see
Alford v.
Canada (Attorney General)
(1997),
1997 CanLII 868 (BC SC)
, 31 B.C.L.R. (3d) 228 (S.C.) per
Brenner J. at 235 and 236.

[30]

Any doubt on an application under
s.19(24)(a) is to be resolved in favour of allowing the pleadings to stand.  see

Dempsey
at paras. 27‑28;

Hunt

at p. 980; and
Citizens of
Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress

(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.)
at p. 276
.

[31]

The requirements for dismissal under Rule 19(24)(b) on the ground that
the claim is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious were thoroughly
canvassed  by Romilly J. in
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc.

in the following terms:

46.   The authorities provide little
guidance as to what constitutes pleadings that are “unnecessary”, “scandalous”,
“frivolous” or “embarrassing”.  However some principles do emerge.

47.   Irrelevancy
and embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it
is difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc
. (1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.).  An “embarrassing”
and “scandalous” pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it will involve the
parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the action by
involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v. Dumas Hotels
Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (B.C.C.A.).  An allegation which is
scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to the proceedings.  It will
only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College of Dental
Surgeons of B.C. v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499 (B.C.C.A.).  A pleading
is “unnecessary” or “vexatious” if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s
cause of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts v. Harrigan
,

1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
, [1992] B.C.J. No. 86 (Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.).  A pleading that is superfluous will
not be struck out if it is not necessarily unnecessary or otherwise
objectionable:
Lutz v.

Canadian Puget Sound Lumber and Timber Co.
(1920),
28 B.C.R 39 (C.A.)
.  A pleading is “frivolous” if it is obviously
unsustainable, not in the sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because
of the doctrine of estoppel:
Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd. et al.,

[1992]
B.C.J. No. 1567
, (6 July 1992), Prince George Registry 20714 (B.C.S.C.).

[32]

Applications to dismiss claims on the ground
that the specific issues identified in the pleadings have been previously and
finally determined in litigation between the same parties by a competent court
or on the ground that the issues should have been determined by the parties
exercising reasonable diligence in that prior action should be brought pursuant
to this Rule.  These will collectively be considered claims barred by issue
estoppel or cause of action estoppel, referred to as the doctrine of
res
judicata.

[33]

An application to dismiss a claim as an abuse of process pursuant
to Rule 19(24)(d) will succeed where the applicant can establish the Court process is being used dishonestly or unfairly, for some
ulterior or improper purpose or that there have been multiple or successive
related proceedings that are likely to cause vexation or oppression:
Budgell
,

Young v. Borzoni et al.
,
2007 BCCA 16
at para.
65
; and
Lawrence et
al. v. Sandilands
,
2003 BCSC 211
at para.
95

[34]

Rule 19 (24)(d) codifies the Court’s inherent
jurisdiction to strike claims that amount to an abuse of the process.  In
Babavic v. Babowech
,
[1993] B.C.J. No. 1802 (S.C.)

Baker J. cited with approval the statement from I.H.  Jacob, “The Inherent
Jurisdiction of the Court” (1970), 23 Current Legal Problems, at 40-41:

[The principle
of abuse of process] connotes that the process of the Court must be used
properly, honestly and in good faith, and must not be abused.  It means that the
Court will not allow its function as a court of law to be misused, and it will
summarily prevent its machinery from being used as a means of vexation or
oppression in the process of litigation.  Unless the Court had power to
intervene summarily to prevent the misuse of legal machinery, the nature and
function of the Court would be transformed from a court dispensing justice into
an instrument of injustice.

[35]

In
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,

2003 SCC 63
, [2003] 3 S.C.R.  77

the Supreme Court of Canada refused to
reverse or relax the requirement that the parties to the former and current
litigation be the same before invoking the doctrines of
res judicata.
The
Court went on, however, to describe the nature and extent of the Courts’
jurisdiction to dismiss as abusive claims that amount to relitigation of an
issue previously determined:

37   In the context that interests us here,
the doctrine of abuse of process engages “the inherent power of the Court to
prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would ... bring the
administration of justice into disrepute” (
Canam Enterprises Inc. v. Coles

(2000),
2000 CanLII 8514 (ON CA)
, 51 O.R. (3d) 481 (C.A.), at para.
55
, per Goudge J.A., dissenting
(approved [2002] 3 S.C.R.  307,
2002 SCC 63
)).  Goudge J.A. expanded on
that concept in the following terms at paras.  55-56:

The doctrine of
abuse of process engages the inherent power of the Court to prevent the misuse
of its procedure, in a way that would be manifestly unfair to a party to the
litigation before it or would in some other way bring the administration of
justice into disrepute
.  It is a flexible doctrine unencumbered by the
specific requirements of concepts such as issue estoppel.
[Internal
citation omitted].

One
circumstance in which abuse of process has been applied is where the litigation
before the Court is found to be in essence an attempt to relitigate a claim
which the Court has already determined.

[Emphasis in original.]

As Goudge J.A.’s comments indicate,
Canadian courts have applied the doctrine of abuse of process to preclude
relitigation in circumstances where the strict requirements of issue estoppel
(typically the privity/mutuality requirements) are not met, but where allowing
the litigation to proceed would nonetheless violate such principles as judicial
economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of
justice.  [....]

38   … the doctrine of abuse of process has
been extended beyond the strict parameters of res judicata while borrowing much
of its rationales and some of its constraints.  It is said to be more of an
adjunct doctrine, defined in reaction to the settled rules of issue estoppel
and cause of action estoppel, than an independent one (internal citation
omitted).  The policy grounds supporting abuse of process by relitigation are
the same as the essential policy grounds supporting issue estoppel [D.J.  Lange,

The Doctrine of Res Judicata in Canada
(2000) at pp.  347-48]:

The two policy grounds, namely, that there
be an end to litigation and that no one should be twice vexed by the same
cause, have been cited as policies in the application of abuse of process by
relitigation.  Other policy grounds have also been cited, namely, to preserve the
Courts’ and the litigants’ resources, to uphold the integrity of the legal
system in order to avoid inconsistent results, and to protect the principle of
finality so crucial to the proper administration of justice.

39   The
locus classicus
for the
modern doctrine of abuse of process and its relationship to res judicata is [
Hunter
v. Chief Constable of the West Midlands Police
,
[1982] A.C.  529 (H.L.)
],
aff’g
McIlkenny v. Chief Constable of the West Midlands,
[1980] Q.B.  283
(C.A.).  At the Court of Appeal, Lord Denning M.R.  endorsed non-mutual issue
estoppel.  ....

40   On appeal to the House of Lords, Lord
Denning’s attempt to reform the law of issue estoppel was overruled, but
the higher court reached the same result via the doctrine of abuse of process.
Lord Diplock stated, at p. 541:

The abuse of
process which the instant case exemplifies is the initiation of proceedings in
a court of justice for the purpose of mounting a collateral attack upon a final
decision against the intending plaintiff which has been made by another court
of competent jurisdiction in previous proceedings in which the intending
plaintiff had a full opportunity of contesting the decision in the Court by
which it was made.  ....

42
The attraction of the doctrine of
abuse of process is that it is unencumbered by the specific requirements of
res
judicata
while offering the discretion to prevent relitigation, essentially
for the purpose of preserving the integrity of the Court’s process.
[....]

[Emphasis
added.]

43   .... I believe that abuse of process is
a doctrine much more responsive to the real concerns at play.  In all of its
applications, the primary focus of the doctrine of abuse of process is the
integrity of the adjudicative functions of courts.  Whether it serves to
disentitle the Crown from proceeding because of undue delays [internal citation
omitted], or whether it prevents a civil party from using the Courts for an
improper purpose [internal citation omitted], the focus is less on the interest
of parties and more on the integrity of judicial decision making as a branch of
the administration of justice.  ....

51   Rather than focus on the motive or
status of the parties, the doctrine of abuse of process concentrates on the
integrity of the adjudicative process.  Three preliminary observations are
useful in that respect.  First, there can be no assumption that relitigation
will yield a more accurate result than the original proceeding.  Second, if the
same result is reached in the subsequent proceeding, the relitigation will
prove to have been a waste of judicial resources as well as an unnecessary
expense for the parties and possibly an additional hardship for some witnesses.
Finally, if the result in the subsequent proceeding is different from the
conclusion reached in the first on the very same issue, the inconsistency, in
and of itself, will undermine the credibility of the entire judicial process,
thereby diminishing its authority, its credibility and its aim of finality.

52   ... There
may be instances where relitigation will enhance, rather than impeach, the
integrity of the judicial system, for example: (1) when the first proceeding is
tainted by fraud or dishonesty; (2) when fresh, new evidence, previously
unavailable, conclusively impeaches the original results; or (3) when fairness
dictates that the original result should not be binding in the new context.
....

[36]

That broad jurisdiction has been considered by
our Court of Appeal in
Roeder v. Lang Michener Lawrence & Shaw
,
2007
BCCA 152
, 67 B.C.L.R. (4th) 301 and
Skender v. Farley,

2007 BCCA 629
, 289 D.L.R. (4
th
)
111.  In the latter case the plaintiff, having failed to establish a
contractual claim to title to property subsequently sued his solicitor,
alleging that the solicitor had failed follow instructions in drafting the
conveyance.  At the first trial the Court had heard the evidence of the
solicitor as a witness and concluded the solicitor had done as he had been
instructed.  The subsequent action against the solicitor was dismissed on the
grounds that the plaintiff was urging upon the Court a finding at “complete variance” with the findings at the first trial.  The
Court held that such a result would be an abuse of process.

ANALYSIS

[37]

On the defendant’s application it falls to me to
examine the statement of claim to see whether the material facts set out would,
if proved, complete all the constituent elements of causes of action known in
law.  Having attempted to read the pleadings in the light most favourable to
the plaintiff and after setting aside matters that are not open to relitigation
I cannot find in the pleadings a cause of action against either Tse or Chan.

The claim against Tse

[38]

Tse’s only involvement in the events said to
have given rise to Ng’s claim was as buyer’s agent in relation to the offer
made to purchase the duplex on April 13, 2008.  Ng suggests he should have
been told Tse had a business association with Parmar or Chan.  Ng does not
specifically allege that he suffered damages as a result of non-disclosure of
the business associations.

[39]

Ng alleges that Tse acted for a legitimate
buyer.  Ng does not suggest that the offer was a fraud.  He says, obliquely,
that Tse misrepresented some fact in relation to the offer to purchase, without
identifying the alleged misrepresentation.  He suggests Tse was complicit in
the failure to arrange inspections and thereby kept the duplex off the market
between the time of the offer and the collapse of the sale on May 1,
2008.

[40]

These claims are founded, first, upon the
supposition that Tse owed a duty of care to Ng and that some damages flowed
from the breach of that duty, and second, upon the proposition that Ng himself
was a victim of the failure of the transaction, rather than its author.

[41]

Ng does not set out a basis for concluding that
Tse had a duty to disclose those associations to him.  That material element of
the claim is not pleaded.

[42]

Wedge J. found that the April 13, 2007
offer to purchase was not a legitimate offer and that the purported purchaser was
“likely Mr. Ng, who was attempting to pressure Mr. Parmar to rectify
any deficiencies he had identified without having to first pay the final
instalment on the contract”.  Ng seeks a finding at complete variance with
those findings.

[43]

Ng has tested that finding on appeal.  This is
not an instance where relitigation will enhance the integrity of the judicial
system.  The first proceeding was not tainted by fraud or dishonesty, other
than that of Ng.  It was not suggested on appeal nor is it suggested now that
there is new, previously unavailable, evidence that conclusively impeaches the
original results.  Fairness certainly does not dictate that the original result
should not be binding.  The claim against Tse amounts to an abuse of process of
the court and is dismissed with costs.

The Claim Against Chan

[44]

The first claim against Chan, the escrow claim,
is also founded upon an allegation dismissed by Wedge J. – that Ng paid
$20,000 to Manjit as a deposit that was to have been held by Chan but was
released.  In relation to the escrow claim, Ng again seeks a finding at
complete variance with the findings at the first trial that the funds were not
received by Manjit.

[45]

Not only is Ng’s escrow claim an abuse of the
process of the Court but it is an abuse that was anticipated and against which
Ng was warned by Wedge J. when she insisted that an accounting of all
payments to Manjit would be made at the trial before her.  The claim in
relation to the $20,000 deposit is dismissed as an abuse of the process of the
court.

[46]

The remaining claim against Chan is more
difficult to address, as it is vague and poorly described.  Ng alleges a breach
of the fiduciary and contractual obligations owed to him by Chan, acting as his
real estate agent.  The breaches appear to consist of concealing or failing to
disclose his business associations with the other parties, recommending the
April 13, 2008 offer and failing to arrange for inspection once the offer
had been accepted.

[47]

The latter two allegations are clearly dependent
upon Ng establishing facts at complete variance with the findings of
Wedge J. It is not open to Ng to advance a claim founded upon the
legitimacy of the April 13, 2008 offer.
Here, as
in
Foreman v. Niven,
2009 BCSC 1476
the
plaintiff’s claim is founded on the loss of an opportunity which the court in
previous proceedings found was not made out.

[48]

For reasons set out
above,
relitigation of that issue will not enhance the
integrity of the judicial system.  To the contrary, to permit Ng to relitigate
the legitimacy of his fraudulent conduct is likely to bring the integrity of
the judicial system into disrepute.

[49]

Even after dismissal of claims dependent upon
the legitimacy of the April 13, 2008 offer, there remains the question
whether Ng has any surviving claim against Chan arising out of the allegation
that Chan failed to make disclosure of the alleged relationship with Tse,
Parmar or Manjit.

[50]

I assume for the purposes of this application
that Ng might be able to establish that Chan failed to disclose material
information to him (although both the nature of the relationship and its
materiality will be in issue).  I further assume that Ng might be able to
establish the failure amounted to a breach of a duty of loyalty and full
disclosure owed by a listing agent and that such duty is fiduciary in nature
(although the real estate agent will not be a fiduciary for all purposes).
Even making those assumptions there are two significant obstacles to Ng’s
remaining claim:

(1)    Ng does not claim to have suffered damages as a result of the
non-disclosure other than those damages said to have arise from the failed
transaction of April 13, 2008; and

(2)    Ng cannot seek an equitable remedy without clean hands.

[51]

Upon establishing a breach of a fiduciary duty,
Ng would be entitled to seek damages of a prophylactic or restitutionary
nature; measured, respectively by the profit or benefit accruing to the
defendant or the loss suffered by the plaintiff .
Strother v. 3464920
Canada Ltd.,
2007 SCC 24
, [2007] 2 S.C.R. 177.  The breach will not
result in damages in the absence of either benefit or loss.  As the Supreme
Court of Canada noted in
Canson Enterprises v. Boughton & Co.
,

1991 CanLII 52 (SCC)
, [1991] 3 S.C.R.  534, at p. 578:

In the case of
a mere breach of duty [as opposed to a breach of trust by a fiduciary], the
concern of equity is to ascertain the loss resulting from the breach of the
particular duty.

[52]

Permitting that claim to continue, in the
absence of a viable plea of actual damages and in the circumstances of this
case would permit an abuse of the process of the court.

[53]

Finally, Ng’s claim for damages arising out of
Chan’s alleged breach of a fiduciary duty to make full disclosure is a claim to
equitable relief.  It must be borne in mind that Ng alleges the breach occurred
in the context of a real estate listing complicated by Ng’s own deception and
later false testimony.  While “[e]quity does not demand that its suitors shall
have led blameless lives”, still, where there is an immediate and necessary
relation between the plaintiff’s conduct and that said to be blameworthy on the
part of the defendant, equity will not come to the former’s assistance:
Canson
Enterprises; Parnell v. Viger
,
[2003] O.T.C. 648 (Ont. S.C.J.)
,
(2003)
CarswellOnt 2711 at para. 22
.

[54]

In the case at bar, given the findings of
Wedge J, the continuance of Ng’s claim that Chan breached a fiduciary duty
to him threatens the integrity of the adjudicative process.

[55]

The statement of claim will be struck in its
entirety and the action dismissed, with costs to the defendants.
